introduction-moving-from-scripts-to-tool.core: A script is written for its author; a tool is written for other people. It needs predictable arguments, help text, clean output, correct exit codes and safe behaviour.

first_principles.problem: Personal scripts handed to a team confuse users, break pipelines and occasionally destroy things.
truths: Other users don't know your assumptions.

analogy.title: A sticky note vs. a printed manual
analogy.story: A sticky note is for you, right now. A manual has structure, instructions and warnings for strangers.
analogy.breaks: Not every one-off needs tool-grade polish, but anything shared does.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Teammates and CI can rely on it.

check.q: What's the key difference between a script and a tool?
check.a: A tool is designed for other users and programs, with a predictable interface and behaviour.

the-anatomy-of-a-command-line.core: A command line is a sentence: the program, subcommands (verbs), options (adverbs that change behaviour) and positional arguments (objects). Good tools follow that grammar.

first_principles.problem: Tools with ad-hoc argument orders and meanings force users to memorise quirks.
truths: The shell splits the line into words for the program.
Users carry over expectations from git and kubectl.

analogy.title: Grammar of a sentence
analogy.story: 'kubectl get pods -n prod': subject, verb, object, and a modifier saying where.
analogy.breaks: Quoting and globbing are applied by the shell before your program sees anything.

steps.label: Design
steps.detail: A tool of your own: `mytool deploy SERVICE --env prod`.

check.q: In `kubectl get pods -n prod`, what is `-n prod`?
check.a: An option with a value (namespace) that modifies the command.

the-standards-flags-conventions-and-the-.core: Follow the Unix conventions: short `-v` and long `--verbose` flags, bundling (`-la`), `--help` and `--version`, and `--` to end option parsing.

first_principles.problem: A tool that uses `-help` or can't handle a filename starting with a dash surprises and frustrates users.
derivation: Honour **--** so everything after it is positional.
Use a parsing library that does this for you.

analogy.title: Standard road signs
analogy.story: Drivers instantly understand a stop sign. A custom-shaped sign causes accidents.
analogy.breaks: Some ecosystems (Go's flag package, Java) differ, but consistency within your tool still matters most.

example.title: Deleting a file called -rf
example.outcome: the tool behaves the way users expect.

check.q: What does `--` mean on a command line?
check.a: End of options: everything after it is treated as positional arguments.

configuration-precedence-the-hierarchy-o.core: Settings come from several layers. The common order is flags > environment variables > project config > user config > system config > defaults. The most specific source wins.

first_principles.problem: Users can't tell which setting is in effect when a tool reads config from many places inconsistently.
truths: More specific intent should override general defaults.
derivation: Then **env vars** (good for CI and containers).

analogy.title: Dress code layers
analogy.story: The company has a default, your team overrides it, and today's meeting overrides both.
analogy.breaks: Secrets shouldn't go in flags, because they show up in process lists and shell history.

example.title: Region resolution
example.scenario: How the AWS CLI picks a region.

steps.label: UX
steps.detail: Offer `mytool config show` to print the effective values and their sources.

check.q: Why do env vars typically override config files?
check.a: They are set closer to the specific run (CI, container), so they carry more specific intent.

output-formatting-humans-vs-machines.core: Humans want readable tables and colour; programs want stable structured data. Provide both: pretty by default on a TTY, and `--output json` for scripts. Send data to stdout and messages to stderr.

first_principles.problem: Scripts that parse human-formatted output break whenever a column is added or colours get mixed in.
truths: A program can detect whether stdout is a terminal.
Mixing logs into stdout corrupts pipelines.
derivation: Use a **table or colour on a TTY**.
Send **data to stdout** and **logs and progress to stderr**.

analogy.title: A menu vs. an order ticket
analogy.story: Customers read a styled menu; the kitchen needs a terse, standardised ticket.
analogy.breaks: JSON output becomes an API, so changing it breaks users. Version it carefully.

example.title: Listing services
example.scenario: The same data shown both ways.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Humans and scripts each get what they need.

code.text:
svc list                 # pretty table
svc list -o json | jq '.[] | select(.healthy==false) | .name'

check.a: To stderr, so they don't pollute data piped from stdout.

interactive-safety-and-the-yes-flag.core: Destructive actions should require confirmation when run interactively, with a `--yes` or `--force` flag for automation. If there's no TTY and no --yes, refuse rather than guess.

first_principles.problem: One mistyped command destroys a production database, or the confirmation prompt hangs a CI job forever.
derivation: Prompt for confirmation on **destructive operations**, ideally by retyping the resource name.
Skip the prompt with **--yes** in CI.

analogy.title: A two-key missile launch
analogy.story: Something irreversible takes deliberate double confirmation, not one accidental press.
analogy.breaks: If prompts appear too often, people learn to type 'y' without reading. Keep them for truly destructive actions.

example.title: Dropping a database

steps.label: Behaviour
steps.detail: In CI without --yes it exits 2 with a message, and never hangs.

code.text:
$ dbctl drop orders-prod
This will permanently destroy 'orders-prod'. Type the name to confirm: _

$ dbctl drop orders-prod --yes   # CI

example.outcome: humans are protected and automation still works.

check.q: What should a tool do if a prompt is needed but there's no TTY?
check.a: Fail with a clear error telling the user to pass --yes, rather than hang or proceed.

exit-code-hygiene.core: Exit 0 only when the tool truly succeeded, and use distinct non-zero codes for distinct failure types. Callers and CI depend on them.

first_principles.problem: A tool prints 'ERROR' but exits 0, so the pipeline carries on and deploys something broken.
truths: Exit codes are the machine-readable result.
Scripts branch on codes, not on text.
Codes above 128 mean the process died from a signal.

analogy.title: Traffic lights for scripts
analogy.story: Green (0) means go. Distinct reds tell the caller why it stopped.
analogy.breaks: Exit codes are a single byte (0–255), so keep the meanings simple.

steps.label: Use
steps.detail: Monitoring can tell 'down' (3) apart from 'checker broke' (1).

code.text: sys.exit(0 if healthy else 3)  # 3 = unhealthy, 1 = couldn't check

check.q: What does exit code 130 usually mean?
check.a: Terminated by SIGINT (128 + 2), for example Ctrl+C.

signal-handling-graceful-shutdowns.core: Catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to stop cleanly: finish or roll back the current step, release locks and exit with the right code. SIGKILL can't be caught.

first_principles.problem: A Ctrl+C or a Kubernetes pod stop leaves half-written files and stale locks behind.
truths: Processes are asked to stop with signals.
SIGTERM is the polite request; SIGKILL follows after a grace period.
derivation: Set a **stop flag** and finish the current unit of work.

analogy.title: Closing time at a shop
analogy.story: When the bell rings (SIGTERM), serve the current customer, lock the till and leave. You don't vanish mid-sale.
analogy.breaks: If cleanup takes longer than the grace period, SIGKILL interrupts it anyway.

example.title: A batch uploader
example.scenario: Stops between files, never in the middle of one.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No half-uploaded files, and the lock is always released.

code.text:
stop = False
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda *_: globals().update(stop=True))
for f in files:
    if stop: break
    upload(f)
release_lock()

points: Finish the unit, then clean up.

check.q: Why handle SIGTERM in containerised tools?
check.a: Orchestrators send SIGTERM to stop pods, and you get a short grace period to shut down cleanly.

putting-it-all-together-the-cli-engineer.core: A production CLI passes a checklist: library-parsed arguments, help, layered config, human and machine output, safety prompts, honest exit codes and graceful signal handling.

first_principles.problem: Individual practices are easy to forget, and a checklist makes quality repeatable.
truths: Each item protects either a user or a pipeline.
derivation: **Output**: TTY vs JSON, stdout vs stderr.

analogy.title: A pilot's pre-flight checklist
analogy.story: Experienced pilots still run the list, because skipping one item can be fatal.
analogy.breaks: The checklist is a minimum. Real users will still find edge cases.

example.title: Reviewing a teammate's tool

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Three gaps found before users found them.

example.outcome: every tool ships at the same quality bar.

check.q: Name three checklist items for a production CLI.
check.a: For example: a parsing library with --help, JSON output to stdout with logs on stderr, and correct exit codes.
